senses: The drift of a ship or aeroplane in a leeward direction.
A varying degree or amount of freedom or flexibility.
An adverse discrepancy or variation in a cumulative process, usually in the phrase make up leeway.
ety: From lee (“side away from the wind”) + way.
examples: I don't think we have a lot of leeway when it comes to proper formatting.

senses: one who receives a pension; a pensioner
ety: From pension + -ary.

senses: An expert in mental illness, especially with reference to legal ramifications.
A psychiatrist.
ety: Borrowed from French aliéniste, from aliéné (“insane”).

senses: A female anchorite. A woman who chooses to withdraw from the world to live a solitary life of prayer and contemplation.
ety: From Middle English ankres, ankerisse, anchoryse; equivalent to anchor + -ess.

senses: A unit of measure of volume transport, used in oceanography, equal to 1 million cubic metres per second.
ety: From Norwegian Sverdrup. After Harald Sverdrup (1888–1957), Norwegian oceanographer and meteorologist.

senses: A European robin, Erithacus rubecula.
An American robin, Turdus migratorius.
ety: From Middle English redbreste, equivalent to red + breast.
examples: I felt comforted by the song of the redbreast, and I thought I felt less lonely and deserted as long as I heard the merry notes of the thrush.

senses: A kind of equid in ancient Mesopotamia (probably a donkey-onager cross).
ety: Learned borrowing from Sumerian 𒀲𒋙𒀭 (^(anše)kunga₂ /⁠kunga⁠/).

senses: A knitted wrist covering
ety: From wrist + -er.

senses: Able to tolerate various saltwater concentrations.
ety: From eury- + haline.

senses: Similar to a pig.
ety: From Middle English porcine, partly from Middle French porcin (from Old French [Term?]) and partly from its etymon, Latin porcīnus, from porcus (“pig”).

senses: Leiurus quinquestriatus, an extremely venomous scorpion of the family Buthidae.
ety: From death + stalker.

senses: A public holiday or feast day in Italy, Portugal, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Italian, Catalan, Portuguese, and Maltese festa. Doublet of fete, fiesta, feast, and fest.

senses: A socialist ideology of cooperation and collective advancement that formed the basis of socioeconomic policies in Tanzania in the 1960s.
A village built according to this ideology, with central homes and school surrounded by communal farmland.
ety: Borrowed from Swahili ujamaa (“brotherhood, extended family”), from jamaa (“family”), from Arabic جَمَاعَة (jamāʕa, “group (of people)”).
examples: She told him the gift was in keeping with the spirit of ujamaa, or cooperative economics, one of the seven principles of Kwanzaa.

senses: An American feline carnivore (Leopardus pardalis, syn. Felis pardalis) covered with blackish ocellated spots and blotches which are variously arranged.
ety: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

senses: The act of causing to rot; the anaerobic splitting of proteins by bacteria and fungi with the formation of malodorous, incompletely oxidized products.
Rotten material.
ety: First attested between 1350 and 1400 from Middle English putrefaccioun, from Old French putrefaccïon, from Latin putrefactiō, from putrefactus, perfect passive participle of putrefaciō (“become rotten”)

senses: A short Japanese sword, built like the katana but with a shorter blade
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 小太刀 (kodachi, literally “small tachi”).

senses: Any major regional biological community such as that of forest or desert.
All the genomes of such a community.
ety: From bio- + -ome.

senses: A person who dashes; a fast runner.
That which dashes or agitates.
A dashboard or splashboard.
ety: From dash + -er.

senses: To withdraw, retract (something said).
To cause something not to have been said; to make it so that one never said something (since this is physically impossible, usually in the subjunctive).
ety: From Middle English unseyen, unseien, from Old English onseċġan (“to deny, renounce”), from Proto-West Germanic *andasaggjan (“to unsay, renounce, deny”), equivalent to un- + say. Cognate with Dutch ontzeggen (“to deny”), German entsagen (“to renounce, abjure”).
examples: There are some things I'd like to unsay... to my boss... right before he decided to fire me.

senses: The blunt head of a jousting-lance.
A small, rounded hill.
ety: From Old French morne, morné, etc.

senses: A rhesus macaque.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi बंदर (bandar).

senses: A fluid confined in a nanoscale structure.
A nanoliquid.
ety: From nano- + fluid.

senses: The process of weaving unspun vegetable fibers to make a basket.
Baskets collectively.
ety: From basket + -ry.

senses: The establishment of a cause, origin, or reason for something.
The study of causes or causation.
ety: Borrowed from Latin aetiologia. By surface analysis, aetio- + -logy. Doublet of aetiologia.

senses: One who, or that which, houses.
A house music track.
ety: From Middle English housere, equivalent to house + -er.
examples: Federal aid for foster care - in effect a houser of last resort for children from troubled families - may also be legitimately described as an entitlement.
They thought they had busted a moonshiner or a houser of illegal aliens, but what was really below their feet was beyond their wildest imaginations!
Social work and gerontological literature for the most part have omitted Haniet Tubman's role as a houser of the aged.

senses: The action of dropping something, in certain children's games.
ety: From drop + -sies.

senses: seaward, towards the sea.
ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian makai (“seaward”).
examples: There are plenty of lots for sale — ranging from $30,000 to $60,000 for an acre that’s mauka (toward the mountain), and $100,000 or much higher for land that’s makai (toward the sea).

senses: A single strand of man-made fiber
ety: From mono- + filament.

senses: Literal interpretation or understanding; adherence to the exact letter or precise significance, as in interpreting or translating.
The style of art portraying a subject as literally and accurately as possible.
ety: From literal + -ism.
examples: The two main forms of literalism are ergism and orthodoxy.

senses: Impressive, top-notch or outstanding.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Malay kilat (“lightning-quick, (slang) impressive”).

senses: A fork-shaped instrument or device, specifically the forked structure between two fingers of a glove.
The wishbone or furculum of birds
The frog of the hoof of the horse and allied animals.
The combination of the card immediately above and the one immediately below a given card.
ety: Borrowed from French fourchette.

senses: A final exam that young adults (aged 18 or 19) take at the end of their secondary education in certain European countries.
ety: Borrowed from Latin mātūra.

senses: The quality or state of being neurotic
ety: From neurotic + -ism.
examples: Your neuroticism is getting out of hand.
Eysenck has suggested the three dimensions of neuroticism, psychoticism and introversion-extraversion.

senses: One who hates or fears strangers or foreigners.
ety: From xeno- + -phobe. From Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange”), + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

senses: Of, or having to do with matrimony and marriage.
ety: From Middle French matrimonial, also matrimony + -al.

senses: Like a cushion: comfortable, soft, yielding.
Having cushions; provided with cushions.
Used as a cushion.
ety: From cushion (noun) + -y (adjectival suffix). First attested in 1830–1840.

senses: Capable of, or suitable for, being licensed.
ety: From license + -able.

senses: The situation where goods, especially jewellery, must be returned by the retailer if not successfully sold.
ety: Short for approbation.
examples: The goods were delivered on appro.

senses: To have two team members, horses, etc., finish first and second in the same event.
ety: From American Spanish quiniela (“sporting bet or pool”); US from 1942.
examples: Smith provided the winner of twenty-one Mares Produce Stakes and quinellaed the event nine times.
Gai quinellaed the Doncaster in 1997 with Secret Savings and All Our Mob.
Not only did he win his first Cup with the 30/1 chance Tawriffic, but in the finest Cummings′ tradition he quinellaed the race with Super Impose.

senses: To take part in kitesurfing.
ety: From kite + surf.
